author: Daniel Sheehan
title: Former CFCC trustee gets settlement after suing board - NewsBreak
text:
By Daniel Sheehan ,
19 hours ago
A former Cape Fear Community College Board of Trustees member has been awarded a settlement three years after suing the board.
Former CFCC Trustee Ray Funderburk’s June 2023 lawsuit, which alleged that board actions against him violated his constitutional rights, has been settled for $265,000, according to a news release from the college. He was removed from the board during a special meeting on March 8, 2023, less than a year into his four-year term.
Previous coverage: Former CFCC Board of Trustees member sues board alleging misconduct by leaders
Funderburk was removed for failing to discharge the duties of a board member and allegations that he attempted to influence an instructor to change the grade of a high school student who had failed an online course at the community college, according to the filing. He sought $25,000 in damages in the initial filing.
Funderburk agreed to the settlement amount with CFCC’s insurance carrier.
“This action was taken to resolve the matter efficiently and does not represent any admission of liability by the Board of Trustees or anyone at the college,” the school said in a statement.
At Funderburk’s first meeting in July 2022, he was the sole vote against raising CFCC President Jim Morton’s salary from $286,000 to $322,584. Following the vote, Funderburk told the media that he couldn’t “in good faith, make a decision when I didn’t have what I considered to be all the facts.”
The lawsuit alleged that CFCC Trustee Bill Cherry, who served as the board’s chair at the time, told Funderburk “not to talk to the liberal media,” according to the filing.
During Funderburk’s removal hearing, Trustee Jason McLeod said that Funderburk had made comments that were “unbecoming of a trustee and reflect negatively on the college” at a Black Student Forum on Feb. 1, 2023.
Funderburk had questioned why media had not been allowed at the event, where students shared stories of “discrimination, racial slurs and overt aggression.”
McLeod said that Funderburk’s comments “implied that CFCC had something to hide.” McLeod noted that the media had not been invited to the forum to create a safe environment where students would feel welcome to share their experiences.
Funderburk described his comments about the media as a “gentle criticism” of the school’s policy.
Daniel Sheehan covers New Hanover County for the StarNews. Reach him at dsheehan@usatodayco.com .
This article originally appeared on Wilmington StarNews: Former CFCC trustee gets settlement after suing board
